newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: TALKS TODAY OVER BHP RESTRUCTURE
Steel Unions and the ACTU are holding talks in Melbourne today with the head of BHP's steel division, Ron McNeilly, about the economic impact of the division's restructure.
BHP is closing down steel making operations in Newcastle and winding back manufacturing plants around the country at the cost of more than 3,000 jobs.
Andrew Whiley from the Australian Workers Union says thousands more jobs will be lost in service industries unless affected regions are compensated.
The Combined Steel Unions and the ACTU have launched a campaign to ensure regional economies affected by the restructure are compensated.
Mr Whiley says today's talks are focussing on Newcastle.
MEASLES JABS URGED AFTER OUTBREAK IN NZ
Parents are being urged to ensure their children are immunised against measles, following the admission to hospital of two babies with measles linked to an outbreak in New Zealand.
The New South Wales Health Department says one of the two infected baby boys, has contracted pneumonia and is on a ventilator.
Spokesman Mark Gold says the Department's concerned the outbreak could spread, and is advising parents to protect their children from the disease by ensuring they're immunised.
He says the immunisation rates in New South Wales are extremely low at around 53 per cent.
Mr Gold says the close proximity to New Zealand means New South Wales is susceptible to outbreaks in that country.

He says New Zealand authorities have reported more than 800 cases of measles over the past few weeks, and the highly contagious nature of measles means there's a strong chance it will spread throughout New South Wales.
PROPERTY DEVELOPER GROLLO ACQUITTED
The long-running conspiring trial, involving property developer Bruno Grollo, and two former employees, came to a dramatic conclusion yesterday.
A Melbourne County Court jury returned a not guilty verdict, after almost five days of deliberations.

The jury found Mr Grollo, Robert Howard and John Flanagan not guilty of conspiring to pervert the course of justice and conspiring to bribe, arising out of an alleged attempt to sabotage a multi-million dollar tax investigation.
The courtroom exploded with emotion as the verdict was returned, with family and friends of the trio cheering and weeping.
Mr Grollo gripped the railing surrounding the dock, and tried to hold back tears as he looked over to his wife.
Mr Grollo said he'd undergone "relentless persecution", since being charged in August 1993.
He said he was happy the ordeal was finally over but still couldn't understand why the trial was permitted to run for more than a year.
Mr Grollo said his lawyers had told him the case would take three months and it had taken almost 13 months.
"Some guy giving some copper seven grand which had nothing to do with me and it's cost me $10-million and 12 months in court," he said.
ELECTRICITY PRIVATISATION OPPOSED IN NSW
There appears to be growing opposition within the New South Wales Government over plans to privatise the electricity industry.
A meeting of the Treasurer's Caucus Committee yesterday unanimously supported a motion opposing the sale.
This follows last week's threat by 26 Government backbenchers to cross the floor if the matter doesn't go to the state Labor conference in October.
Labor backbencher Pat Rogan says the message from yesterday's meeting is that the Government faces certain defeat at the next election if it goes ahead with the plan.
He says MPs and union leaders are receiving this message from their branch members and Labor supporters in the Labor heartland.
TEXTILE INDUSTRY WORRIED ABOUT TARIFF CUTS
The textile, clothing and footwear industry is anxious about the contents of the Industry Commission's draft report on the future role of tariffs for the industry.
The report is due for release on Monday.
Graham McIntosh, of Adelaide-based Consolidated Apparel Industries, says the industry has almost halved tariffs over the past decade.
He says that has caused a 30 per cent drop in the number of jobs in the industry.
Mr McIntosh says under OECD requirements, T-C-F tariffs are meant to be abolished by 2010.
But he says the industry doesn't want tariff protection to fall below 10 per cent until at least 2005.
QLD TO PERSIST WITH ATTEMPT TO HAVE FILM BANNED
Queensland Attorney-General, Denver Beanland, is hopeful he will succeed in his appeal to have the film Salo banned from cinemas throughout Australia.
The Office of Film Literature Classification rejected his intial bid to have the film's current R rating overturned.
The film features scenes of sexual degradation and torture.
Mr Beanland says he understands his attempt to have the film banned only narrowly failed.
He says he is hoping for more success from the appeal.
